title: Psychiatry
topics: Psychiatric assessment and mental state exam

notes.h: Psychiatric assessment and the mental state examination
notes.body:
A psychiatric history covers:
- presenting complaint and its history
- past psychiatric history, including self-harm and admissions
- medical history and medication
- family history
- personal history: development, education, relationships, work, forensic history
- substance use
- premorbid personality
- current social circumstances.
A collateral history from family, the GP or previous notes is often essential.

The mental state examination (MSE) is a structured, objective snapshot of the person during the interview:
- Appearance and behaviour: self-care, eye contact, rapport, psychomotor agitation or retardation, abnormal movements.
- Speech: rate, volume, quantity, tone, flow (pressured, slowed, mute).
- Mood and affect. Mood is the sustained emotional state the patient reports, recorded in their words. Affect is the observed, moment-to-moment expression: its range, reactivity and congruence. It may be flat, blunted or labile.
- Thought form: flight of ideas (rapid, linked by puns or rhymes; seen in mania); loosening of associations, knight's move thinking and word salad (schizophrenia); circumstantiality (gets there eventually); tangentiality (never gets there); perseveration; neologisms; thought block.
- Thought content: preoccupations, obsessions (intrusive, recognised as one's own, resisted), overvalued ideas, delusions, and suicidal or homicidal ideation. A delusion is a fixed, false belief held with conviction despite contrary evidence and not explained by the person's cultural or religious background.
- Perception: a hallucination is a perception without an external stimulus; an illusion is a misperception of a real stimulus; a pseudohallucination is experienced as inside the mind. Note the modality. Second-person voices fit mood disorder; third-person running commentary is a first-rank symptom.
- Cognition: orientation, attention and memory. Use a formal tool where indicated (e.g. MoCA, ACE-III).
- Insight: does the person recognise illness and accept treatment? Record it as partial or graded, not simply yes or no.

Risk assessment covers risk to self (suicide, self-harm, neglect), to others, and from others (exploitation, abuse), plus risks to children and driving. NICE NG225 (2022) on self-harm advises against using risk scales or tools to predict suicide or to decide who gets treatment. Use a needs-based, collaborative safety plan instead.

Physical assessment matters. Organic causes include thyroid disease, delirium, epilepsy, intoxication, B12 deficiency and space-occupying lesions. Baseline investigations depend on presentation.

Worked illustration: a man sits motionless, answers in monosyllables after long pauses, describes his mood as 'empty', and hears a voice saying 'you're rotten'. Write this up as psychomotor retardation, poverty of speech, subjectively low mood with restricted affect, and a mood-congruent second-person auditory hallucination.

Exam pitfalls:
- Recording interpretation ('paranoid') instead of description.
- Confusing mood (subjective) with affect (observed).
- Calling an illusion or a pseudohallucination a hallucination.
- Omitting risk or physical health.

A depressive episode (ICD-11; DSM-5-TR) involves low mood or loss of interest or pleasure (anhedonia) for at least two weeks, most of the day, nearly every day. Accompanying symptoms include:
- poor concentration
- worthlessness or excessive guilt
- hopelessness
- recurrent thoughts of death or suicide
- sleep and appetite change
- psychomotor agitation or retardation
- fatigue.
DSM-5-TR requires five of nine symptoms, including depressed mood or anhedonia. Severity reflects symptom number and functional impact, and psychotic features (typically mood-congruent delusions of guilt, poverty or nihilism) indicate severe illness.

Aetiology combines biological, psychological and social factors:
- Biological: genetic loading, monoamine dysregulation, HPA-axis overactivity, inflammation.
- Psychological: Beck's negative cognitive triad (self, world, future).
- Social: life events and adversity. Brown and Harris (1978) identified vulnerability factors in women: lack of a confiding relationship, three or more children under 14 at home, no employment outside the home, and loss of the mother before age 11.

Differentials:
- bipolar depression (ask about previous highs)
- hypothyroidism, anaemia, Cushing's, Parkinson's disease, malignancy
- medication (e.g. corticosteroids) and alcohol
- dementia in older adults
- grief (consider prolonged grief disorder in ICD-11).

Management (NICE NG222, 2022):
- Severity: 'less severe' corresponds broadly to PHQ-9 below 16, 'more severe' to 16 or above.
- Less severe: guided self-help, group CBT or behavioural activation, individual CBT, BA or IPT, counselling, or short-term psychodynamic therapy. Antidepressants are not routinely first-line unless the person prefers them.
- More severe: combined individual CBT and an antidepressant is the most effective first choice. Alternatives include individual CBT or BA alone, or an antidepressant alone.
- Drug classes: SSRIs (usually first choice), SNRIs, mirtazapine (an α₂-antagonist), tricyclics (dangerous in overdose) and MAOIs (dietary tyramine interactions).
- Safety: suicidal thoughts can increase early on, especially under 25, so review sooner. Look for hyponatraemia (older adults on SSRIs) and bleeding risk (SSRIs with NSAIDs or anticoagulants). Serotonin syndrome is a risk when serotonergic drugs are combined. Discontinuation symptoms can be severe and prolonged, so taper gradually.
- Continue antidepressants for at least six months after remission. Longer if there is a high risk of relapse.
- ECT for severe, life-threatening depression (e.g. refusal of food and fluids) or catatonia, or when other treatments have failed.

Applied point: postnatal depression is screened for with the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. Ask about thoughts of harm to the baby, and refer early to perinatal mental health services.

Exam pitfalls:
- Missing bipolar disorder before starting an antidepressant.
- Not asking directly about suicide. Asking does not increase risk.
- Forgetting organic causes and physical health.

Anxiety becomes a disorder when it is excessive, persistent and impairing.

- Generalised anxiety disorder (GAD): excessive, hard-to-control worry about many things, with restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, muscle tension and poor sleep. DSM-5-TR requires six months.
- Panic disorder: recurrent unexpected panic attacks (palpitations, breathlessness, dizziness, fear of dying or losing control), followed by persistent worry about further attacks or avoidance. It is often accompanied by agoraphobia, avoidance of places where escape or help is difficult.
- Social anxiety disorder: fear of scrutiny or humiliation. Specific phobia: fear of a particular object or situation.
- Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD): obsessions (intrusive, unwanted thoughts, images or urges, recognised as one's own) and compulsions (repetitive acts that reduce distress). ICD-11 and DSM-5 classify it separately from the anxiety disorders.
- PTSD: after an extremely threatening or horrific event, re-experiencing in the present (flashbacks, nightmares), avoidance, and a persistent sense of current threat (hypervigilance, startle). ICD-11 complex PTSD adds problems with affect regulation, negative self-concept and relationships, typically after prolonged or repeated trauma.

Mechanisms include amygdala hyperreactivity, fear conditioning, avoidance that maintains anxiety, catastrophic misinterpretation of bodily sensations in panic (Clark's model), and genetic and temperamental vulnerability.

Exclude organic causes: hyperthyroidism, hypoglycaemia, phaeochromocytoma (rare), arrhythmia, asthma, caffeine, stimulants, and alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal.

Management uses stepped care (NICE CG113 for GAD and panic, with separate guidance for social anxiety, OCD and PTSD):
- Step 1: identification, psychoeducation and active monitoring.
- Step 2: low-intensity interventions (guided or unguided self-help, psychoeducational groups), delivered by NHS Talking Therapies.
- Step 3: high-intensity CBT or applied relaxation (GAD), or CBT (panic), or drug treatment. An SSRI is the first-line drug class, and NICE names sertraline first for GAD. SNRIs and pregabalin are alternatives.
- Step 4: specialist care for complex or refractory cases.
- Benzodiazepines are not recommended for GAD or panic, except very short-term in a crisis, because of dependence.
- OCD: CBT with exposure and response prevention (ERP), and/or an SSRI or clomipramine.
- PTSD (NICE NG116, 2018): trauma-focused CBT. Offer EMDR to adults when PTSD follows non-combat trauma and has lasted over three months. Single-session debriefing is not recommended.

Worked illustration: a 30-year-old has four attacks a month and now avoids trains. Diagnose panic disorder with agoraphobia. Check thyroid function, and do an ECG if palpitations suggest arrhythmia. Offer CBT with graded exposure. An SSRI is an option, with a warning that anxiety may briefly worsen when starting.

Exam pitfalls:
- Prescribing benzodiazepines long-term.
- Confusing obsessions with delusions: insight is usually retained in OCD.
- Missing comorbid depression or alcohol use.

Psychosis is loss of contact with reality: delusions, hallucinations and disorganised thought or behaviour. It occurs in schizophrenia, schizoaffective and delusional disorders, mood disorders with psychotic features, and substance-induced and organic states.

Schizophrenia (ICD-11) requires at least two characteristic symptoms for at least one month, one of which is a core feature:
- core features: persistent delusions, persistent hallucinations, thought disorder, or experiences of influence, passivity or control
- other features: negative symptoms, grossly disorganised behaviour, psychomotor disturbance (including catatonia).
DSM-5-TR requires continuous signs for six months, including one month of active symptoms.

Schneider's first-rank symptoms:
- auditory hallucinations (third-person voices, running commentary, thought echo)
- thought alienation (insertion, withdrawal, broadcast)
- passivity experiences (made feelings, impulses or actions; somatic passivity)
- delusional perception.
They are suggestive but not pathognomonic.

Symptom domains:
- Positive: delusions, hallucinations.
- Negative: avolition, alogia, anhedonia, blunted affect, social withdrawal.
- Cognitive: attention, working memory and executive function.
Cognitive and negative symptoms drive long-term disability.

Epidemiology and risk: lifetime risk is about 1%. Onset is usually from late adolescence to the early thirties, earlier in men. Risk factors are family history (monozygotic concordance around 40–50%), heavy or high-potency cannabis use, urban upbringing, migration and minority status, obstetric complications and childhood adversity.

Neurochemistry: in the dopamine hypothesis, mesolimbic overactivity produces positive symptoms. Blockade in other pathways explains side effects: nigrostriatal (extrapyramidal effects) and tuberoinfundibular (hyperprolactinaemia). Reduced mesocortical activity is linked to negative and cognitive symptoms. NMDA receptor hypofunction (the glutamate hypothesis) is also implicated.

Assessment: full history and MSE, risk, drug screen, bloods, and neuroimaging or EEG where indicated. Differentials include delirium, temporal lobe epilepsy, autoimmune encephalitis (e.g. anti-NMDA receptor) and substance-induced psychosis.

Management (NICE CG178, 2014):
- Refer to early intervention in psychosis services.
- Offer an oral antipsychotic, chosen with the patient according to side-effect profile, plus CBT for psychosis and family intervention.
- Side effects: extrapyramidal (acute dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia), metabolic (weight, glucose, lipids), hyperprolactinaemia and QTc prolongation. Monitor weight, glucose or HbA1c, lipids, blood pressure and ECG.
- Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is an emergency: hyperthermia, rigidity, autonomic instability, altered consciousness and raised CK.
- Treatment-resistant schizophrenia (no response to at least two antipsychotics, at least one non-clozapine second-generation drug): clozapine. Mandatory blood monitoring guards against neutropenia and agranulocytosis. Also watch for myocarditis, severe constipation (ileus risk), hypersalivation and seizures. Levels rise when a person stops smoking.
- Address physical health: life expectancy is substantially reduced in severe mental illness.

Exam pitfalls:
- Diagnosing schizophrenia without excluding substances and organic causes.
- Treating first-rank symptoms as diagnostic on their own.
- Forgetting clozapine constipation and the effect of smoking changes.

Bipolar disorder involves episodes of mania or hypomania, usually alternating with depression.
- Bipolar I: at least one manic episode.
- Bipolar II: hypomania plus major depression, never mania.
- Cyclothymia: persistent sub-threshold mood instability.

Mania is elevated, expansive or irritable mood with increased energy for at least a week (or any duration if admission is needed). Features include reduced need for sleep, pressured speech, flight of ideas, grandiosity, distractibility, disinhibition and risk-taking, sometimes with mood-congruent psychotic features. Hypomania is milder (DSM-5-TR: at least four days), with no psychosis or marked impairment. Lifetime prevalence of bipolar I is about 1%, onset is usually in late adolescence or early adulthood, and heritability is high.

Differentials:
- stimulants and corticosteroids
- hyperthyroidism and frontal lesions
- schizoaffective disorder
- ADHD and emotionally unstable personality disorder, where mood shifts are briefer and reactive.
Always ask depressed patients about past highs. Antidepressant monotherapy can provoke a manic switch.

Management (NICE CG185):
- Acute mania: stop or taper any antidepressant. Offer an antipsychotic (e.g. haloperidol, olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone). If ineffective, try another, then consider adding lithium, then valproate (subject to restrictions). Manage risk, using the Mental Health Act if needed.
- Bipolar depression: quetiapine, olanzapine with fluoxetine, or lamotrigine, plus psychological therapy.
- Long-term: lithium is the first-line mood stabiliser and is linked to lower suicide risk. Alternatives are valproate (restricted), olanzapine or quetiapine. Add psychoeducation, relapse-signature planning, CBT and family work.

Lithium:
- It has a narrow therapeutic index. Take levels about 12 hours post-dose.
- Monitor renal and thyroid function, calcium and weight.
- Toxicity: coarse tremor, ataxia, dysarthria, vomiting and diarrhoea, confusion, seizures, arrhythmia.
- Levels are raised by dehydration, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers and thiazides.
- Long-term effects: hypothyroidism, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, chronic kidney disease, hyperparathyroidism.
- Pregnancy: a small increased risk of cardiac malformation (e.g. Ebstein's anomaly) calls for specialist perinatal planning.

Valproate is highly teratogenic and causes neurodevelopmental harm. MHRA measures from January 2024 say it must not be started in anyone under 55 unless two specialists independently document that no other effective or tolerated treatment exists, or that the reproductive risks do not apply. Those who can become pregnant must meet the Pregnancy Prevention Programme conditions. (A February 2025 MHRA update removed the two-specialist review for men already taking valproate; the rule for starting it is unchanged.) Lamotrigine needs slow titration because of the risk of serious rash.

Applied illustration: a man on lithium starts an NSAID for gout and develops vomiting, coarse tremor and unsteadiness. Suspect toxicity. Stop both drugs, check the level, U&E and ECG, and give fluids. Severe cases may need haemodialysis.

Exam pitfalls:
- Antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar disorder.
- Forgetting lithium interactions.
- Prescribing valproate without considering pregnancy potential.

ICD-11 distinguishes a harmful pattern of use from dependence. Dependence needs at least two of the following over 12 months (or continuous use for one month):
- impaired control over use
- use taking increasing precedence despite harm
- physiological features: tolerance, withdrawal, or use to avoid withdrawal.
Dependence alone is not a mental disorder under the Mental Health Act 1983 (s1(3)).

Alcohol:
- Units = volume (ml) × ABV (%) ÷ 1,000. A 750 ml bottle of 13.5% wine ≈ 10.1 units.
- UK Chief Medical Officers (2016): no more than 14 units a week regularly, spread over three or more days.
- Screening: AUDIT-C, full AUDIT (20 or more suggests possible dependence), CAGE.
- Withdrawal starts within hours: tremor, sweating, anxiety, tachycardia. Seizures may occur, typically in the first two days. Delirium tremens (confusion, hallucinations, autonomic instability) peaks around days 2–3 and can be fatal.
- Manage withdrawal with a long-acting benzodiazepine (e.g. chlordiazepoxide), symptom-triggered or on a fixed reducing regimen.
- Wernicke's encephalopathy (thiamine deficiency): confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia or nystagmus, often incomplete. Give urgent parenteral thiamine. Untreated, it can progress to Korsakoff syndrome (anterograde amnesia, confabulation).
- Relapse prevention (NICE CG115): acamprosate (glutamate/GABA modulation), naltrexone (opioid antagonist that reduces reward from drinking) or disulfiram (aldehyde dehydrogenase inhibitor that causes an aversive reaction), plus psychosocial support.

Opioids:
- Overdose: pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression, reduced consciousness. Give naloxone (a competitive antagonist). It is short-acting, so toxicity can recur; observe.
- Withdrawal: dilated pupils, yawning, lacrimation, rhinorrhoea, piloerection, cramps, diarrhoea. It is rarely life-threatening.
- Opioid substitution: methadone (full μ agonist) or buprenorphine (high-affinity partial agonist, which can precipitate withdrawal if started too soon after a full agonist). Add psychosocial support, take-home naloxone, needle exchange, BBV testing and hepatitis B vaccination.

Other substances:
- Cannabis: psychosis risk, especially high-potency forms.
- Stimulants: cardiovascular events and psychosis.
- Nitrous oxide: functional B12 deficiency and myelopathy. It has been a Class C drug under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971 since November 2023.

Behaviour change:
- Prochaska and DiClemente's stages of change: precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action, maintenance, with relapse a normal part of the cycle.
- Motivational interviewing (Miller and Rollnick): open questions, affirmations, reflections and summaries, and developing discrepancy.
- Brief interventions in primary care reduce hazardous drinking.

Exam pitfalls:
- Giving glucose before thiamine in a malnourished drinker.
- Forgetting re-sedation after naloxone wears off.
- Moralising instead of using harm reduction.

The Mental Health Act 1983 (MHA), as amended in 2007, governs compulsory assessment and treatment of mental disorder ('any disorder or disability of the mind') in England and Wales. A learning disability counts for longer-term sections only with abnormally aggressive or seriously irresponsible conduct. Dependence on alcohol or drugs alone is excluded.

Civil sections:
- s2, assessment: up to 28 days. AMHP (approved mental health professional) or nearest relative applies; two medical recommendations, one s12-approved. Tribunal application within 14 days.
- s3, treatment: 6 months, renewable for 6 months and then yearly. Appropriate treatment must be available. The AMHP cannot proceed if the nearest relative objects (displacement is possible).
- s4, emergency: 72 hours, one doctor plus an AMHP.
- s5(2): a doctor holds an informal inpatient for up to 72 hours. s5(4): a nurse's holding power, up to 6 hours. Neither applies in A&E.
- s135(1): magistrate's warrant to enter premises. s136: police remove a person from anywhere except a home to a place of safety, for up to 24 hours (police cells barred for under-18s since 2017).
- s17: leave. s17A: community treatment order.
- Forensic: s37 hospital order, s41 restriction order, s47 and s48 prison transfers.

Treatment:
- s63 covers treatment for mental disorder and its consequences, such as nasogastric feeding in anorexia (B v Croydon HA 1995).
- s58: after three months, medication needs consent or a SOAD certificate.
- s58A: no ECT for a capacitous refuser, except under s62 in an emergency.
- s117: free aftercare after s3 or s37.

MHA versus MCA:
- The Mental Capacity Act 2005 is capacity-based (best interests).
- The MHA is risk-based, can override capacitous refusals of psychiatric treatment, and cannot be used for unrelated physical illness (Re C 1994; St George's v S 1998).
- An incapacitous patient objecting to psychiatric admission is usually detained under the MHA, not DoLS.

Reform: the Mental Health Act 2025 received Royal Assent on 18 December 2025, but only limited provisions are in force. From 18 February 2026 (two months after Royal Assent, under the Act itself), restricted patients can be conditionally discharged with conditions amounting to a deprivation of liberty, and some prison and immigration-detention transfer provisions changed. From 6 April 2026 (Commencement No. 1 Regulations, SI 2026/385), Human Rights Act duties extend to private providers of certain services (s51), and a review of CQC notification of under-18 inpatients is required (s52). The main civil reforms are to be commenced in stages over several years:
- detention criteria based on serious harm and therapeutic benefit
- limits on s3 detention of autistic people and people with a learning disability
- a nominated person replacing the nearest relative
- a shorter initial s3 period (three months rather than six)
- advance choice documents and more tribunal access.
Check legislation.gov.uk for current commencement.

Exam pitfalls:
- Using s5(2) in A&E.
- Using the MHA for unrelated physical illness.
- Stating the 2025 reforms as if fully in force.

Child and adolescent psychiatry:
- ADHD: persistent inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity, present before 12 (DSM-5-TR), in at least two settings, with impairment. NICE NG87 (2018): start with education, environmental modifications and ADHD-focused parent training (especially for under-5s). From age 5, if impairment persists, methylphenidate (a CNS stimulant blocking dopamine and noradrenaline reuptake) is first-line, then lisdexamfetamine. Monitor height, weight, pulse and blood pressure.
- Autism: social communication and interaction difficulties plus restricted, repetitive behaviours and sensory differences from early development. Diagnosis is multidisciplinary. There is no medication for core features.
- Conduct disorder and oppositional defiant disorder: parent training first, and screen for safeguarding concerns.
- Depression (NICE NG134, 2019): psychological therapy first. If medication is needed, fluoxetine with therapy and close monitoring.
- Anorexia (NICE NG69, 2017): eating-disorder-focused family therapy for young people. Assess medical risk with the RCPsych MEED guidance (2022), which replaced MARSIPAN and Junior MARSIPAN: watch for bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia, electrolyte disturbance and refeeding syndrome.
- Law: Gillick-competent children can consent. Relying on parental consent to override a young person's refusal is discouraged; use the MHA or the court. Parents cannot authorise a deprivation of liberty for 16–17-year-olds (Re D [2019] UKSC 42). Under-18s detained under the MHA need an age-appropriate environment (s131A).

Old-age psychiatry:
- Dementia subtypes:
  - Alzheimer's disease (most common): insidious memory loss.
  - Vascular dementia: stepwise decline.
  - Lewy body dementia: fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, REM sleep behaviour disorder and severe antipsychotic sensitivity.
  - Frontotemporal dementia: early behavioural or language change.
- Assessment: collateral history, cognitive tests (ACE-III, MoCA), and bloods for reversible contributors (FBC, U&E, LFTs, calcium, glucose, thyroid function, B12, folate). Imaging where indicated.
- Treatment (NICE NG97, 2018): acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, galantamine, rivastigmine) for mild to moderate Alzheimer's. Memantine (NMDA antagonist) for moderate disease when those are unsuitable, or for severe disease. Anti-amyloid antibodies (lecanemab, donanemab) are licensed in the UK, but NICE's guidance recommends against their routine NHS use on cost-effectiveness grounds; check for any later reappraisal.
- Behavioural and psychological symptoms: non-drug approaches first. Antipsychotics only for severe distress or risk, short-term, because they increase stroke and mortality risk.
- Delirium: acute, fluctuating inattention, which may be hyperactive, hypoactive or mixed. Screen with the 4AT. Treat causes (infection, drugs, metabolic disturbance, pain, constipation, retention, withdrawal), reorientate and minimise sedation (NICE CG103).
- Late-life depression may mimic dementia ('pseudodementia'). Suicide risk is high in older men.
- Adult safeguarding: section 42 enquiries under the Care Act 2014.

Exam pitfalls:
- Labelling delirium as dementia.
- Giving antipsychotics in Lewy body dementia.
- Assuming parents can always override a competent teenager.

cards.f: List the main headings of the mental state examination.
cards.b: Appearance and behaviour; speech; mood and affect; thought form; thought content; perception; cognition; insight. Risk is usually recorded alongside.

cards.f: Mood vs affect?
cards.b: Mood is the sustained emotional state the patient reports, recorded in their words. Affect is the observed, moment-to-moment emotional expression (range, reactivity, congruence).

cards.f: Define a delusion.
cards.b: A fixed, false belief held with conviction despite evidence to the contrary, and not explained by the person's cultural, religious or educational background.

cards.f: Hallucination vs illusion?
cards.b: A hallucination is a perception without an external stimulus. An illusion is a misperception of a real external stimulus (e.g. seeing a coat on a door as a person).

cards.f: What is an overvalued idea?
cards.b: A strongly held, emotionally charged belief that dominates a person's life but is not held with delusional fixity and is understandable in context (e.g. body shape beliefs in anorexia).

cards.f: Flight of ideas vs loosening of associations?
cards.b: In flight of ideas, thoughts race with understandable links (puns, rhymes, distractions), typically in mania. In loosening of associations, the links between ideas are lost, typical of schizophrenia.

cards.f: Circumstantiality vs tangentiality?
cards.b: Circumstantial speech includes excessive detail but eventually reaches the point. Tangential speech drifts away and never returns to the point.

cards.f: What are the key features of an obsession?
cards.b: An intrusive, unwanted thought, image or urge that the person recognises as a product of their own mind and usually tries to resist or neutralise.

cards.f: What does NICE NG225 (2022) say about risk assessment tools after self-harm?
cards.b: Do not use risk assessment tools or scales to predict future suicide or self-harm, or to decide who receives treatment or discharge. Focus on a needs-based psychosocial assessment and safety plan.

cards.f: What is a pseudohallucination?
cards.b: A vivid perceptual experience that the person recognises as coming from inside their own mind, rather than perceived as external, real space.

cards.f: Minimum duration for a depressive episode in ICD-11 and DSM-5-TR?
cards.b: At least two weeks, present most of the day, nearly every day.

cards.f: What are the two core symptoms, at least one of which DSM-5-TR requires for major depression?
cards.b: Depressed mood and markedly diminished interest or pleasure (anhedonia).

cards.f: What is Beck's cognitive triad?
cards.b: Negative views of the self, the world and the future, maintained by cognitive distortions. It is the basis of CBT for depression.

cards.f: Name Brown and Harris's (1978) vulnerability factors for depression in women.
cards.b: Lack of a confiding relationship; three or more children under 14 at home; no employment outside the home; loss of the mother before age 11.

cards.f: NICE NG222: first-line treatment for more severe depression?
cards.b: Combination of individual CBT and an antidepressant is the most effective first choice. Alternatives include individual CBT or behavioural activation alone, or an antidepressant alone.

cards.f: Why review young adults soon after starting an antidepressant?
cards.b: There may be a short-term increase in suicidal thoughts and agitation, especially under 25, so early review (about a week) and safety planning are advised.

cards.f: Which electrolyte disturbance is a key risk of SSRIs in older adults?
cards.b: Hyponatraemia (via SIADH). Consider checking sodium, especially with diuretics or other risk factors.

cards.f: Clinical features of serotonin syndrome?
cards.b: Neuromuscular hyperactivity (clonus, hyperreflexia, tremor), autonomic instability (fever, tachycardia, sweating, diarrhoea) and altered mental state. It follows combinations of serotonergic drugs.

cards.f: Give two indications for ECT in depression.
cards.b: Severe, life-threatening depression (e.g. refusal of food and fluids, high suicide risk) needing a rapid response; catatonia; or failure of multiple other treatments.

cards.f: Why ask about previous elevated mood before treating depression?
cards.b: Undiagnosed bipolar disorder may present as depression, and antidepressant monotherapy can precipitate mania or rapid cycling.

cards.f: Core features of generalised anxiety disorder?
cards.b: Excessive, uncontrollable worry about multiple everyday matters, with restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, muscle tension and sleep disturbance. DSM-5-TR requires six months or more.

cards.f: Panic disorder vs GAD?
cards.b: Panic disorder involves recurrent, discrete, unexpected surges of intense fear peaking within minutes, plus worry about further attacks. GAD is continuous, diffuse worry without discrete attacks.

cards.f: First-line drug class for GAD according to NICE?
cards.b: An SSRI, with sertraline named as first choice. SNRIs and pregabalin are alternatives. Benzodiazepines are only for short-term crisis use.

cards.f: Why are benzodiazepines not recommended for GAD or panic long-term?
cards.b: They cause tolerance, dependence and withdrawal, impair cognition and coordination, and are associated with poorer long-term outcomes in panic disorder.

cards.f: What is exposure and response prevention?
cards.b: A CBT technique for OCD. Patients are gradually exposed to feared triggers while refraining from compulsions, so anxiety habituates and beliefs are disconfirmed.

cards.f: What are the three core symptom clusters of PTSD in ICD-11?
cards.b: Re-experiencing the event in the present; avoidance of reminders; and a persistent sense of current threat (hypervigilance, exaggerated startle).

cards.f: What distinguishes complex PTSD in ICD-11?
cards.b: Core PTSD symptoms plus disturbances in self-organisation: affect dysregulation, negative self-concept, and difficulties in relationships. It usually follows prolonged or repeated trauma.

cards.f: NICE NG116 recommended psychological treatments for adult PTSD?
cards.b: Trauma-focused CBT. EMDR is offered for PTSD after non-combat trauma lasting over three months. Single-session debriefing is not recommended.

cards.f: Name four organic differentials for anxiety.
cards.b: Hyperthyroidism, hypoglycaemia, cardiac arrhythmia, phaeochromocytoma, asthma or COPD, and caffeine, stimulant or alcohol withdrawal (any four).

cards.f: In Clark's cognitive model, what maintains panic?
cards.b: Catastrophic misinterpretation of bodily sensations (e.g. palpitations interpreted as a heart attack) increases anxiety, which intensifies the sensations in a vicious circle. Safety behaviours prevent disconfirmation.

cards.f: Name Schneider's first-rank symptoms.
cards.b: Third-person auditory hallucinations, running commentary, thought echo; thought insertion, withdrawal and broadcast; passivity of feelings, impulses, actions or somatic function; delusional perception.

cards.f: Give five negative symptoms of schizophrenia.
cards.b: Avolition, alogia (poverty of speech), anhedonia, blunted affect and social withdrawal (asociality).

cards.f: ICD-11 minimum duration for schizophrenia?
cards.b: Characteristic symptoms for at least one month. DSM-5-TR requires six months of disturbance, including one month of active symptoms.

cards.f: Which dopamine pathway is linked to positive symptoms?
cards.b: The mesolimbic pathway. Overactivity there is thought to underlie hallucinations and delusions, and D2 blockade there mediates antipsychotic efficacy.

cards.f: Antipsychotic blockade in which pathways causes extrapyramidal effects and hyperprolactinaemia?
cards.b: Nigrostriatal blockade causes extrapyramidal effects. Tuberoinfundibular blockade causes hyperprolactinaemia, because dopamine normally inhibits prolactin release.

cards.f: Define treatment-resistant schizophrenia and its treatment.
cards.b: Inadequate response to at least two antipsychotics, at least one a non-clozapine second-generation drug, given adequately. Clozapine is indicated.

cards.f: Why is regular blood monitoring mandatory with clozapine?
cards.b: To detect neutropenia and agranulocytosis early, a potentially fatal adverse effect. Treatment is stopped if neutrophil counts fall below set thresholds.

cards.f: Name three clozapine adverse effects other than agranulocytosis.
cards.b: Myocarditis or cardiomyopathy, severe constipation and ileus, hypersalivation, seizures, weight gain and metabolic syndrome (any three).

cards.f: Features of neuroleptic malignant syndrome?
cards.b: Hyperthermia, severe muscle rigidity, autonomic instability, altered consciousness and raised creatine kinase, after starting or increasing an antipsychotic. It is a medical emergency.

cards.f: Why does stopping smoking matter for a patient on clozapine?
cards.b: Smoking induces CYP1A2, which metabolises clozapine. On stopping, clozapine levels can rise sharply and cause toxicity, so levels must be monitored.

cards.f: Bipolar I vs bipolar II?
cards.b: Bipolar I requires at least one manic episode. Bipolar II involves hypomanic episodes plus at least one major depressive episode, with no history of mania.

cards.f: Mania vs hypomania?
cards.b: Mania lasts at least a week (or needs admission) and causes marked impairment, sometimes with psychosis. Hypomania is milder, shorter (at least four days in DSM-5-TR), and without psychosis or marked impairment.

cards.f: First-line long-term mood stabiliser in bipolar disorder?
cards.b: Lithium (NICE CG185), which also has evidence of reducing suicide.

cards.f: When should lithium levels be taken?
cards.b: About 12 hours after the last dose, regularly during initiation and periodically once stable.

cards.f: Name four drug classes that raise lithium levels.
cards.b: NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers and thiazide diuretics. Dehydration also raises levels.

cards.f: Clinical features of lithium toxicity?
cards.b: Coarse tremor, ataxia, dysarthria, nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea, confusion, myoclonus, seizures, arrhythmias and coma.

cards.f: Long-term adverse effects of lithium?
cards.b: Hypothyroidism, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, chronic kidney disease, hyperparathyroidism and hypercalcaemia, weight gain and fine tremor.

cards.f: What did the January 2024 MHRA measures say about starting valproate?
cards.b: It must not be started in new patients under 55 (male or female) unless two specialists independently consider and document that there is no other effective or tolerated treatment, or that the reproductive risks do not apply.

cards.f: First step in managing acute mania in a patient taking an antidepressant?
cards.b: Stop or taper the antidepressant, then start an antipsychotic. Manage risk and consider the setting of care.

cards.f: Why is lamotrigine titrated slowly?
cards.b: To reduce the risk of serious skin reactions, including Stevens–Johnson syndrome. The risk is higher with rapid escalation or co-prescription with valproate.

cards.f: How do you calculate alcohol units?
cards.b: Units = volume (ml) × ABV (%) ÷ 1,000. For example, a 500 ml can of 5% lager = 2.5 units.

cards.f: What is the UK CMO low-risk drinking guideline (2016)?
cards.b: No more than 14 units a week on a regular basis for men and women, spread over three or more days.

cards.f: ICD-11 features of dependence?
cards.b: Impaired control over use; increasing precedence of use over other interests despite harm; physiological features (tolerance, withdrawal, use to relieve withdrawal). Two are needed.

cards.f: Classic triad of Wernicke's encephalopathy?
cards.b: Confusion, ataxia and ophthalmoplegia or nystagmus. The full triad is often absent, so maintain a low threshold for parenteral thiamine.

cards.f: What characterises Korsakoff syndrome?
cards.b: Profound anterograde (and some retrograde) amnesia with confabulation, relatively preserved other cognition. It follows thiamine deficiency, often after untreated Wernicke's.

cards.f: Typical timeline of alcohol withdrawal?
cards.b: Symptoms begin within hours of the last drink. Seizures most often occur within the first two days. Delirium tremens typically appears around 48–72 hours.

cards.f: Mechanisms of acamprosate, naltrexone and disulfiram?
cards.b: Acamprosate modulates glutamate/GABA to reduce craving. Naltrexone is an opioid antagonist that reduces the rewarding effect of alcohol. Disulfiram inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, so acetaldehyde accumulates and drinking becomes unpleasant.

cards.f: Signs of opioid overdose?
cards.b: Pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression and reduced consciousness. Treat with naloxone and airway support, and observe for recurrence because naloxone is short-acting.

cards.f: Methadone vs buprenorphine?
cards.b: Methadone is a full μ-opioid agonist. Buprenorphine is a high-affinity partial agonist with a ceiling on respiratory depression, but it can precipitate withdrawal if given while a full agonist is still active.

cards.f: What are the stages of change (Prochaska and DiClemente)?
cards.b: Precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action and maintenance, with relapse as a common part of the cycle.

cards.f: Section 2 MHA: duration and requirements?
cards.b: Up to 28 days for assessment (and treatment). Application by an AMHP or the nearest relative, with two medical recommendations (one s12-approved). Not renewable.

cards.f: Section 3 MHA: duration?
cards.b: Up to 6 months initially, renewable for 6 months, then for 12 months at a time. Appropriate medical treatment must be available.

cards.f: What is section 5(2)?
cards.b: A doctor's or approved clinician's holding power for an informal hospital inpatient, for up to 72 hours to allow a MHA assessment. It does not apply in A&E.

cards.f: What is section 5(4)?
cards.b: A nurse's holding power. A qualified mental health or learning disability nurse can hold an informal inpatient for up to 6 hours until a doctor attends.

cards.f: What does section 136 allow?
cards.b: Police may remove a person who appears to have a mental disorder and to need immediate care, from any place other than a dwelling, to a place of safety for assessment, for up to 24 hours (extendable by 12).

cards.f: What is the 'three-month rule' in s58?
cards.b: After three months of medication for mental disorder under detention, further medication needs the patient's capacitous consent or a second opinion appointed doctor's certificate.

cards.f: Can ECT be given to a detained patient with capacity who refuses?
cards.b: No. Under s58A a capacitous refusal cannot be overridden, except under s62 for urgent treatment in specified emergencies.

cards.f: What is section 117 aftercare?
cards.b: A joint duty on health and social services to provide free aftercare to people who have been detained under s3, s37 or certain transfer sections, until they no longer need it.

cards.f: Can the MHA authorise treatment of an unrelated physical illness?
cards.b: No. The MHA authorises treatment for mental disorder (including its direct consequences). Unrelated physical treatment needs consent or MCA best interests (e.g. St George's v S 1998).

cards.f: When did the Mental Health Act 2025 receive Royal Assent, and are its main reforms in force?
cards.b: 18 December 2025. Only limited provisions had commenced by mid-2026: deprivation-of-liberty conditions for conditionally discharged restricted patients (18 February 2026) and Human Rights Act duties for certain private providers (6 April 2026, SI 2026/385). The main civil reforms await staged commencement, so check current status.

cards.f: Core features of ADHD?
cards.b: Persistent inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity beyond developmental expectations, beginning in childhood (before 12 in DSM-5-TR), in two or more settings, causing impairment.

cards.f: First-line drug for ADHD in children aged 5 and over (NICE NG87)?
cards.b: Methylphenidate, a CNS stimulant that inhibits dopamine and noradrenaline reuptake, after environmental modifications and support. Monitor height, weight, pulse and blood pressure.

cards.f: Core diagnostic domains of autism?
cards.b: Persistent difficulties in social communication and interaction, plus restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour, interests or activities (including sensory differences), from early development.

cards.f: First-line treatment for anorexia nervosa in young people (NICE NG69)?
cards.b: Anorexia-focused family therapy (FT-AN).

cards.f: What is the MEED guidance?
cards.b: RCPsych 'Medical Emergencies in Eating Disorders' (2022). It replaced MARSIPAN and Junior MARSIPAN for assessing and managing medical risk in eating disorders across all ages.

cards.f: Delirium vs dementia?
cards.b: Delirium is acute, fluctuating, with impaired attention and awareness, usually from a physical cause, and often reversible. Dementia is insidious and progressive, with attention relatively preserved early on.

cards.f: Core features of dementia with Lewy bodies?
cards.b: Fluctuating cognition, recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations, REM sleep behaviour disorder and parkinsonism. There is marked sensitivity to antipsychotics.

cards.f: Mechanism of memantine?
cards.b: Non-competitive NMDA receptor antagonist that reduces glutamate excitotoxicity. Used for moderate (if AChE inhibitors unsuitable) or severe Alzheimer's disease.

cards.f: Why avoid antipsychotics for behavioural symptoms in dementia where possible?
cards.b: They increase the risk of stroke and death, and cause sedation, falls and parkinsonism. Use non-drug approaches first, and antipsychotics only for severe distress or risk, short-term and reviewed.

cards.f: What did Re D (2019) decide?
cards.b: The Supreme Court held that parents cannot consent to arrangements amounting to a deprivation of liberty for a 16- or 17-year-old. Authorisation must come from the court or a statutory scheme.

questions.q: A patient walking home at dusk briefly sees a bin bag as a crouching person, then recognises it correctly. This is best described as:
questions.why: An illusion is a misperception of a real external stimulus. A hallucination occurs without any stimulus.

questions.q: Distinguish (a) mood from affect and (b) a delusion from an overvalued idea. (4 marks)
markScheme: Mood: sustained subjective emotional state reported by the patient
Affect: observed, moment-to-moment emotional expression (range, reactivity, congruence)
Delusion: fixed false belief, held with full conviction despite evidence, not culturally explained
Overvalued idea: strongly held, emotionally charged, understandable belief that dominates life but lacks delusional fixity
questions.modelAnswer: Mood is the person's sustained emotional state as they describe it, recorded in their own words (e.g. 'empty'). Affect is the clinician's observation of emotional expression during the interview, including its range, reactivity and congruence with content. A delusion is a fixed, false belief held with unshakeable conviction despite evidence to the contrary and not explained by the person's culture. An overvalued idea is an intensely held, emotionally loaded belief that dominates behaviour, such as an anorexic person's conviction about their body size. It is comprehensible in context and lacks absolute delusional fixity.

questions.q: A 34-year-old woman presents to A&E after taking an overdose. Outline how you would assess and manage her risk, in line with NICE guidance on self-harm. (5 marks)
markScheme: Ensure medical safety first (physical treatment, toxicity assessment)
Comprehensive psychosocial assessment: circumstances, intent, planning, precautions against discovery, current suicidal ideation, hopelessness
Explore needs and protective factors, mental disorder, substance use, safeguarding (children), social stressors
Do not use risk scales or tools to predict suicide or allocate care (NICE NG225)
Collaborative safety plan, means restriction, follow-up and communication with GP; involve family/carers with consent
questions.modelAnswer: Medical safety comes first: treat the overdose and assess toxicity. Once she is medically fit, a trained clinician should carry out a psychosocial assessment. This covers the events leading up to the overdose, its intent, any planning or precautions against discovery, a final note, current suicidal ideation and hopelessness. It also covers mental disorder, substance use, social stressors, safeguarding (dependent children) and protective factors. NICE NG225 (2022) advises against using risk scales or tools to predict suicide or decide who receives care. Instead, agree a collaborative safety plan, limit access to means, arrange follow-up with mental health services and the GP, and involve family with her consent.

questions.q: You assess Mr Ken Adebayo, 45, on a medical ward. He is unshaven, in a stained gown, and sits very still, making little eye contact. He answers after long pauses in a quiet monotone, with very few words. He says he feels 'dead inside' and that he is 'rotting from the inside, my bowels have stopped, I deserve this'. He reports hearing a man's voice saying 'you're disgusting' when no one is present. He is oriented in time, place and person but struggles to name months backwards. He says doctors are wasting their time on him. (a) Write up his mental state examination using the correct terminology. (b) Give the most likely diagnosis and two differentials. (14 marks)
markScheme: Appearance/behaviour: self-neglect, poor eye contact, psychomotor retardation
Speech: slow, quiet, monotonous, poverty of speech, increased latency
Mood: subjectively 'dead inside'/low
Affect: flat/restricted, congruent
Thought content: nihilistic (Cotard-type) delusion and delusional guilt, mood-congruent
Assess and record suicidal ideation (must be explicitly explored)
Perception: second-person derogatory auditory hallucination, mood-congruent
Cognition: oriented; impaired attention/concentration
Insight: poor (does not accept help)
Diagnosis: severe depressive episode with psychotic features
Differentials: schizoaffective disorder; organic causes (e.g. hypothyroidism, malignancy, delirium); bipolar depression; schizophrenia with depression
Notes need for urgent risk assessment and physical work-up
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Mental state examination
- Appearance and behaviour: a middle-aged man showing signs of self-neglect (unshaven, stained gown). Marked psychomotor retardation, sitting very still. Poor eye contact and limited rapport.
- Speech: increased latency of response, slow, quiet and monotonous, with poverty of speech.
- Mood: subjectively 'dead inside'; objectively depressed.
- Affect: flat or restricted, and congruent with mood.
- Thought form: slowed, with no formal thought disorder evident.
- Thought content: nihilistic delusion that his body is rotting and his bowels have stopped (a Cotard-type delusion), with delusional guilt ('I deserve this'). Both are mood-congruent. Suicidal ideation and thoughts of harm to others must be asked about explicitly and recorded. Hopelessness is evident.
- Perception: second-person derogatory auditory hallucination ('you're disgusting'), mood-congruent.
- Cognition: oriented in time, place and person. Impaired attention and concentration (difficulty reciting months backwards), possibly because of depression, but formal testing is needed.
- Insight: poor. He does not see himself as ill or as benefiting from help.

(b) The most likely diagnosis is a severe depressive episode with psychotic features, given the psychomotor retardation, nihilistic and guilty delusions, and derogatory second-person voices, all congruent with low mood.

Differentials:
- Organic causes, given that he is a medical inpatient: hypothyroidism, malignancy (weight loss and bowel symptoms need investigation), hypoactive delirium, or medication effects.
- Bipolar depression (ask about past elevated mood).
- Schizoaffective disorder or schizophrenia with depression, if psychotic symptoms predate the mood change or persist without it.

He needs urgent risk assessment (high risk with psychotic depression and poor intake), physical investigation, and a review of food and fluid intake. ECT may be indicated if the illness is life-threatening.

questions.q: According to ICD-11 and DSM-5-TR, what is the minimum duration of symptoms for a depressive episode?
questions.why: Both systems require symptoms for at least two weeks, most of the day, nearly every day.

questions.q: Which of the following was identified by Brown and Harris (1978) as a vulnerability factor for depression in women?
options: Loss of the mother before age 11
questions.why: Their vulnerability factors were loss of the mother before 11, three or more children under 14 at home, lack of a confiding relationship and no employment outside the home.

questions.q: Outline the NICE NG222 (2022) approach to a new episode of more severe depression in an adult, including the key safety points when starting an antidepressant. (5 marks)
markScheme: More severe depression: PHQ-9 score 16 or above (broad guide)
First choice: combination of individual CBT and an antidepressant (alternatives: CBT/BA alone, antidepressant alone, IPT etc.)
SSRI usually first-line class; shared decision-making about side effects
Safety: early review (within about 1 week if under 25 or suicide risk) and safety planning
Risks: hyponatraemia, GI bleeding with NSAIDs/anticoagulants, serotonin syndrome, discontinuation symptoms; continue at least 6 months after remission
questions.modelAnswer: More severe depression corresponds broadly to a PHQ-9 score of 16 or above. NICE recommends a combination of individual CBT and an antidepressant as the most effective first choice. Other options, chosen with the patient, include CBT or behavioural activation alone, or an antidepressant alone. An SSRI is usually the first drug class. Review early, within about a week for people under 25 or at increased suicide risk, and agree a safety plan. Warn about initial side effects, hyponatraemia in older adults, bleeding risk with NSAIDs or anticoagulants, serotonin syndrome and discontinuation symptoms. Continue treatment for at least six months after remission and taper gradually.

questions.q: Mr Arthur Doyle, 74, a retired engineer, is brought by his daughter. Over three months he has lost 6 kg, wakes at 4 a.m., has stopped gardening and says he 'can't remember anything any more'. His wife died a year ago. He takes bendroflumethiazide and ibuprofen. On examination he is slow and tearful. He scores poorly on a cognitive screen but often answers 'I don't know'. He says he has thought about 'not waking up' and has been stockpiling tablets. (a) Discuss the differential diagnosis. (b) Outline the immediate and longer-term management, including risks specific to his age and medication. (16 marks)
markScheme: Most likely severe depressive episode (biological features: early waking, weight loss, anhedonia, psychomotor retardation)
Depressive pseudodementia: 'don't know' answers, prominent complaint of memory loss, recent onset
Differentials: dementia (Alzheimer's/vascular) or comorbid; prolonged grief disorder; hypothyroidism; malignancy (weight loss); medication or alcohol; delirium
Investigations: bloods (FBC, U&E incl. sodium, calcium, TFT, B12/folate, glucose), consider imaging/cancer work-up
High suicide risk: older widowed man, plan/stockpiling, hopelessness
Immediate: remove access to means, urgent referral to older adult mental health/crisis team, consider admission, MHA if needed
Treatment: psychological therapy plus antidepressant; consider ECT if life-threatening/refusing food
SSRI risks: hyponatraemia (with thiazide: check sodium), GI bleeding with NSAID (stop ibuprofen or gastroprotection)
Avoid tricyclics given overdose toxicity and anticholinergic effects in elderly
Bereavement support, social isolation, involve daughter, review cognition after mood improves
Safety-net and follow-up; communicate with GP
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The likeliest diagnosis is a severe depressive episode. He has anhedonia, early morning waking, weight loss, psychomotor slowing, tearfulness and suicidal ideation, following bereavement. His memory complaints and frequent 'I don't know' answers suggest depressive pseudodementia: cognitive impairment driven by poor effort and concentration, usually with recent onset and prominent subjective complaint.

Differentials:
- Dementia, or early dementia with comorbid depression. Late-life depression can be a prodrome, so cognition must be reassessed once mood improves.
- Prolonged grief disorder, although biological features and suicidal planning point to depression.
- Physical causes: hypothyroidism, hypercalcaemia, anaemia, and especially malignancy, given the weight loss.
- Hyponatraemia (thiazide), alcohol misuse, and a hypoactive delirium.

Investigations: FBC, U&E with sodium, calcium, thyroid function, B12 and folate, glucose, LFTs, and imaging or cancer investigations as indicated.

(b) Immediate. He has a high suicide risk: an older, recently widowed man with a plan and stockpiled tablets. Remove access to means, with his daughter's help and his consent. Refer urgently to the crisis or older adult mental health team and consider admission. If he refuses and the risk is high, a Mental Health Act assessment may be needed.

Treatment. Combine psychological therapy with an antidepressant. An SSRI or mirtazapine is preferred over tricyclics, which are dangerous in overdose and anticholinergic. SSRIs with a thiazide raise hyponatraemia risk, so check sodium at baseline and early on. SSRIs with an NSAID raise GI bleeding risk, so stop the ibuprofen or add gastroprotection. If he stops eating or drinking, or has psychotic features, ECT may be indicated.

Longer term: bereavement support, tackling isolation (befriending, community groups), involving his daughter, continuing treatment for at least six months after remission (longer in older adults), and repeating cognitive testing after recovery.

questions.q: According to NICE, which drug class is first-line when medication is chosen for generalised anxiety disorder?
questions.why: NICE recommends an SSRI (sertraline first) as the first-line drug. Benzodiazepines are reserved for short-term crisis use, and beta-blockers do not treat GAD.

questions.q: A 40-year-old has taken a benzodiazepine nightly for panic disorder for two years. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Switching to a second benzodiazepine will resolve tolerance
Long-term benzodiazepines are first-line for panic disorder
It should be stopped abruptly to prevent dependence
Withdrawal should be gradual, with CBT offered as the evidence-based treatment
questions.why: NICE does not recommend benzodiazepines for panic disorder. Abrupt cessation risks withdrawal, including seizures, so taper gradually and offer CBT.

questions.q: Compare the clinical features of panic disorder and generalised anxiety disorder. (4 marks)
markScheme: Panic: recurrent, unexpected discrete attacks peaking within minutes
Panic: autonomic symptoms (palpitations, breathlessness, chest pain, dizziness), fear of dying/losing control; anticipatory anxiety/avoidance
GAD: persistent, diffuse, excessive worry about many matters, hard to control
GAD: chronic (≥6 months in DSM-5-TR) with restlessness, fatigue, tension, poor concentration, sleep disturbance
questions.modelAnswer: Panic disorder involves recurrent, unexpected panic attacks: discrete episodes of intense fear peaking within minutes. Symptoms include palpitations, breathlessness, chest tightness, dizziness, and fear of dying or losing control. Between attacks there is persistent worry about further attacks, often with avoidance or agoraphobia. GAD instead involves continuous, diffuse worry about many everyday matters that the person finds hard to control. It lasts at least six months in DSM-5-TR and comes with restlessness, fatigue, muscle tension, irritability, poor concentration and sleep disturbance, without discrete attacks.

questions.q: Describe the core features of obsessive-compulsive disorder and its first-line treatments. (4 marks)
markScheme: Obsessions: intrusive, unwanted, distressing thoughts/images/urges recognised as own
Compulsions: repetitive behaviours or mental acts performed to reduce anxiety or prevent feared outcome; time-consuming/impairing
Psychological: CBT including exposure and response prevention
Pharmacological: SSRI (or clomipramine), often combined with CBT in more severe cases
questions.modelAnswer: OCD is characterised by obsessions: intrusive, unwanted thoughts, images or urges, such as contamination fears or fears of causing harm. The person recognises them as their own and finds them distressing. Compulsions are repetitive behaviours (washing, checking) or mental acts (counting) performed to neutralise anxiety or prevent a feared event. They are time-consuming and impairing, and insight is usually at least partly retained. First-line treatment is CBT with exposure and response prevention. Drug treatment uses an SSRI or clomipramine, combined with CBT in more severe or impairing cases.

questions.q: Ms Leah Rahman, 29, a paramedic, was assaulted at work eight months ago. Since then she has had vivid intrusive memories in which she feels the attack is happening again, nightmares, and avoids the area where it happened. She is constantly on edge and startles easily. She has started drinking most nights 'to sleep'. Her manager asks whether she should have had 'a debriefing session' straight after the incident. (a) What is the diagnosis, and how does it differ from complex PTSD in ICD-11? (b) Outline evidence-based management. (c) Respond to the manager's question. (15 marks)
markScheme: Diagnosis: PTSD (ICD-11) after a threatening event
Features: re-experiencing in the present, avoidance, persistent sense of current threat (hypervigilance, startle)
Complex PTSD adds disturbances in self-organisation (affect dysregulation, negative self-concept, relationship difficulty), usually after prolonged/repeated trauma
Assess comorbidity: depression, alcohol use, suicide risk; occupational impact
Trauma-focused CBT first-line (NICE NG116)
EMDR option for adults with PTSD >3 months after non-combat trauma
Drug treatment (e.g. SSRI/venlafaxine) if preference or psychological therapy not effective/accepted, not as first line over trauma-focused therapy
Address alcohol (AUDIT, brief intervention, avoid self-medication)
Occupational health, phased return, workplace support
Single-session psychological debriefing not recommended; may not help and could be harmful
Active monitoring/support after trauma and screening for later PTSD
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Ms Rahman has PTSD (ICD-11). After an extremely threatening event she has re-experiencing in the present (vivid intrusive memories felt as happening now, and nightmares), avoidance of reminders, and a persistent sense of current threat (hypervigilance, exaggerated startle), lasting months and impairing her. ICD-11 complex PTSD requires these core features plus disturbances in self-organisation: problems with affect regulation, a persistent negative self-concept (shame, worthlessness) and difficulty sustaining relationships. It typically follows prolonged or repeated trauma such as childhood abuse. Her presentation fits PTSD, but these domains should be screened for.

(b) Assessment should cover depression, suicidal ideation, alcohol use (AUDIT), sleep and occupational functioning. NICE NG116 (2018) recommends individual trauma-focused CBT as first-line. EMDR is an option for adults whose PTSD follows non-combat trauma and has lasted over three months, which applies here. Drug treatment, such as an SSRI or venlafaxine, is considered if she prefers it or does not engage with or respond to trauma-focused therapy, not as a routine first-line alternative.

Her drinking to sleep is self-medication. It worsens sleep quality and mood, so offer a brief intervention and, if she is dependent, specialist support. Occupational health can arrange adjustments and a phased return. Support from family and peers is protective.

(c) The manager should be told that NICE does not recommend single-session psychological debriefing for everyone after a traumatic event. Trials have not shown that it prevents PTSD, and some suggest it may cause harm. Good practice is practical support, active monitoring, and screening for persistent symptoms with referral for trauma-focused treatment if they develop. Routine debriefing would not have been the right intervention.

questions.q: Which of the following is a Schneiderian first-rank symptom?
questions.why: Thought broadcasting is a form of thought alienation and a first-rank symptom. Second-person voices are more typical of mood disorder, flight of ideas of mania, and visual hallucinations suggest an organic cause.

questions.q: A patient on clozapine develops a sore throat and fever. What is the most important immediate investigation?
options: Full blood count with differential (neutrophil count)
questions.why: Sore throat and fever may herald neutropenia or agranulocytosis, a potentially fatal adverse effect. An urgent FBC with neutrophil count is needed.

questions.q: Describe the four main dopaminergic pathways and how antipsychotic D2 blockade in each relates to therapeutic and adverse effects. (5 marks)
markScheme: Mesolimbic: overactivity linked to positive symptoms; blockade gives antipsychotic effect
Mesocortical: hypoactivity linked to negative/cognitive symptoms; blockade may worsen these
Nigrostriatal: blockade causes extrapyramidal side effects (dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia)
Tuberoinfundibular: blockade raises prolactin (galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea, sexual dysfunction)
Second-generation drugs' lower D2 affinity/5-HT2A antagonism reduce EPSE risk but increase metabolic effects (overall link)
questions.modelAnswer: Mesolimbic overactivity is linked to positive symptoms, and D2 blockade here produces the antipsychotic effect. Mesocortical underactivity is associated with negative and cognitive symptoms, which blockade may worsen. Nigrostriatal blockade causes extrapyramidal effects: acute dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism and tardive dyskinesia. Tuberoinfundibular blockade removes dopamine's inhibition of prolactin, causing galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea and sexual dysfunction. Second-generation drugs often combine D2 blockade with 5-HT2A antagonism or looser D2 binding. This lowers extrapyramidal risk, but many carry greater metabolic risk.

questions.q: Jordan Price, 21, a second-year student, is brought to his GP by his mother. Over four months he has withdrawn to his room, stopped attending lectures and covered his laptop camera, saying the university is 'putting thoughts into my head through the Wi-Fi'. He hears two voices discussing him in the third person. He smokes high-strength cannabis daily. Physical examination is unremarkable. (a) What symptoms does he describe and what is the differential diagnosis? (b) Outline initial investigations and management. (15 marks)
markScheme: Thought insertion (first-rank symptom) and persecutory delusion
Third-person auditory hallucinations discussing him (first-rank)
Negative symptoms/functional decline (withdrawal)
Differential: first-episode schizophrenia; substance-induced psychotic disorder (cannabis); schizophreniform/acute transient psychosis
Organic differentials: temporal lobe epilepsy, autoimmune encephalitis, thyroid disease, other drugs; mood disorder with psychosis
Risk assessment: self, others, vulnerability, self-neglect
Investigations: urine drug screen, FBC, U&E, LFT, TFT, glucose/HbA1c, lipids, prolactin baseline, ECG; consider neuroimaging/EEG if atypical
Urgent referral to early intervention in psychosis service
Offer antipsychotic chosen with patient on side-effect profile, plus CBTp and family intervention (NICE CG178)
Cannabis: psychoeducation, motivational approach, substance misuse support
Physical health monitoring; support education; involve family with consent
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Jordan describes thought insertion (thoughts put into his head through the Wi-Fi), with a persecutory delusional explanation, and third-person auditory hallucinations of voices discussing him. Both are Schneiderian first-rank symptoms. Social withdrawal and declining function suggest negative symptoms or a prodrome.

Differential diagnosis:
- First-episode schizophrenia: symptoms for over a month (ICD-11), with characteristic features.
- Cannabis-induced psychotic disorder. Daily high-potency cannabis is a strong risk factor, and symptoms persisting during abstinence favour a primary psychosis.
- Schizophreniform or acute and transient psychotic disorder.
- A mood disorder with psychotic features.
- Organic causes: temporal lobe epilepsy, autoimmune (e.g. anti-NMDA receptor) encephalitis, thyroid disease, and other drugs such as stimulants.

(b) Assess risk to himself (suicide, self-neglect), to others (especially if he acts on persecutory beliefs) and from others.

Investigations: urine drug screen; FBC, U&E, LFTs, thyroid function, calcium, glucose or HbA1c, lipids and baseline prolactin; weight, BMI, blood pressure and ECG before antipsychotics. Consider neuroimaging or EEG if there are atypical features such as confusion, seizures or focal signs.

Management (NICE CG178): refer urgently to the early intervention in psychosis service. Offer an oral antipsychotic, chosen with Jordan according to side effects (metabolic, extrapyramidal, prolactin, sedation), with regular physical health monitoring. Offer CBT for psychosis and family intervention, and give the family information and carer support. Address cannabis use non-judgementally with psychoeducation and motivational interviewing, and link him with substance misuse services. Support his education through the university disability or mental health service. Agree a crisis plan. If he refuses assessment and the risk is high, a Mental Health Act assessment may be considered.

questions.q: 'The dopamine hypothesis provides an adequate explanation of schizophrenia.' Critically evaluate this statement. (20 marks)
markScheme: States the hypothesis: excess subcortical (mesolimbic) dopamine transmission underlies positive symptoms
Pharmacological evidence: antipsychotic efficacy correlates with D2 affinity; amphetamine can induce psychosis
Imaging evidence: increased presynaptic dopamine synthesis/release in striatum
Revised hypothesis (aberrant salience; final common pathway; mesocortical hypofunction for negative symptoms)
Limitations: negative and cognitive symptoms poorly explained and poorly treated by D2 blockade
Treatment resistance (~a substantial minority) and clozapine's efficacy despite low D2 occupancy
Delay in therapeutic response despite rapid receptor blockade
Glutamate/NMDA hypofunction (ketamine/PCP model; anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis)
Neurodevelopmental model, genetics (polygenic), environmental risks (cannabis, urbanicity, migration, adversity)
Social and psychological models (stress-vulnerability, cognitive models of psychosis)
Biopsychosocial integration: dopamine as final common pathway
Reasoned conclusion: necessary part but insufficient explanation
questions.modelAnswer:
The dopamine hypothesis proposes that excess dopaminergic transmission, particularly in mesolimbic and striatal pathways, causes psychotic symptoms. It is one of psychiatry's most influential theories, and it explains part, but not all, of schizophrenia.

Evidence in favour:
- The clinical potency of first-generation antipsychotics correlates with their D2 receptor affinity.
- Dopamine-releasing drugs such as amphetamine can induce psychosis in healthy people and worsen it in patients.
- PET studies show raised presynaptic dopamine synthesis and release in the striatum of people with schizophrenia and in those at high risk.
- The revised hypothesis frames dopamine dysregulation as a 'final common pathway' that assigns aberrant salience to ordinary stimuli, giving rise to delusions and hallucinations. It explains positive symptoms well.

Limitations:
- Negative and cognitive symptoms, which drive long-term disability, respond poorly to D2 blockade. The revised model attributes them to mesocortical hypofunction, an acknowledgement that a simple 'excess' theory is incomplete.
- A substantial minority of patients are treatment-resistant despite adequate D2 blockade. Clozapine, the most effective drug, has relatively low D2 occupancy, implying other mechanisms.
- Receptor blockade is immediate, yet clinical response often builds over days to weeks.
- Ketamine and phencyclidine, NMDA receptor antagonists, reproduce positive, negative and cognitive features, and anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis can present with psychosis. These support a glutamate hypothesis in which NMDA hypofunction may drive dopamine dysregulation downstream.
- Genetic studies show a polygenic architecture involving synaptic and immune genes. Environmental factors (obstetric complications, cannabis, urban upbringing, migration, childhood adversity) and the neurodevelopmental model point to causes upstream of dopamine.
- Psychological models, such as stress-vulnerability and cognitive accounts of how anomalous experiences are appraised, explain content and course, and underpin effective CBT for psychosis and family interventions.

Conclusion: dopamine dysregulation is probably a necessary proximate mechanism for positive psychotic symptoms. It is not an adequate explanation of schizophrenia as a whole. An integrated biopsychosocial model is needed, with dopamine as a final common pathway influenced by glutamatergic, genetic, developmental and social factors.

questions.q: A woman stable on lithium for bipolar disorder is started on a new medicine for hypertension and two weeks later develops coarse tremor, diarrhoea and ataxia. Which medicine is most likely responsible?
questions.why: ACE inhibitors reduce renal lithium clearance and raise levels, causing toxicity. Thiazides, ARBs and NSAIDs do the same.

questions.q: List the clinical features of lithium toxicity and outline the principles of its management. (5 marks)
markScheme: GI: nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea
Neurological: coarse tremor, ataxia, dysarthria, confusion, myoclonus, seizures, coma
Stop lithium (and interacting drugs); urgent serum lithium level, U&E/renal function, ECG
Supportive care: IV fluids, correct electrolytes, monitor; avoid nephrotoxins
Severe toxicity (high levels, neurological signs, renal impairment): specialist/toxicology advice and haemodialysis
questions.modelAnswer: Toxicity causes GI symptoms (nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea) and neurological signs: coarse tremor, ataxia, dysarthria, confusion, hyperreflexia or myoclonus, and in severe cases seizures, arrhythmias and coma. Management: stop lithium and any interacting drugs (NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, thiazides). Check the serum lithium level urgently, with renal function, electrolytes and an ECG. Give supportive care with IV fluids to maintain hydration and renal clearance, and monitor neurological status. Seek toxicology advice. Haemodialysis is used for severe toxicity, particularly with renal impairment or serious neurological features.

questions.q: Ms Chloe Martin, 28, has bipolar I disorder and has been well for three years on sodium valproate, prescribed before current restrictions. She tells her GP she and her partner hope to start a family 'soon'. She is not using contraception. She had one severe postpartum-like manic episode after a period of sleep loss at 22. (a) Explain the concerns about valproate and the relevant regulatory position. (b) Discuss how her treatment should be managed before and during pregnancy and after delivery. (16 marks)
markScheme: Valproate highly teratogenic: neural tube defects and other major malformations
Neurodevelopmental disorders (lower IQ, autism, ADHD) after exposure in utero
MHRA: must not be used in those who can become pregnant unless Pregnancy Prevention Programme conditions met; annual specialist review/risk acknowledgement form
January 2024 measures: new patients under 55 require two specialists; existing patients reviewed
Urgent advice on effective contraception now; do not stop valproate abruptly
Urgent referral to psychiatry/perinatal mental health for preconception planning
Switch to alternative (e.g. an antipsychotic such as quetiapine/olanzapine, or lithium with specialist monitoring) before conception
Lithium: small cardiac malformation risk, level changes in pregnancy and post-partum, neonatal monitoring
High risk of postpartum psychosis/relapse, especially with history of mania and sleep disruption
Perinatal plan: specialist obstetric and perinatal mental health care, sleep protection, early warning signs, birth plan
Breastfeeding considerations and neonatal monitoring discussed with specialists
Shared decision-making, documentation, folic acid advice
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Valproate is highly teratogenic. Exposure in pregnancy carries a substantially raised risk of major congenital malformations, such as neural tube defects, and of neurodevelopmental disorders (lower IQ, autism, ADHD) in a large proportion of exposed children. The MHRA says valproate must not be used in girls and women who can become pregnant unless the conditions of the Pregnancy Prevention Programme are met. These include highly effective contraception, specialist review at least annually and a signed risk acknowledgement form. In bipolar disorder it must not be used in pregnancy. Measures from January 2024 restrict new prescribing for anyone under 55 to cases where two specialists document that there is no alternative, and require existing patients to be reviewed.

(b) Ms Martin, who is trying to conceive, is at serious risk. The GP should:
- advise effective contraception immediately while treatment is reviewed
- warn her not to stop valproate abruptly, because relapse risk is high
- refer urgently to her psychiatrist and perinatal mental health services for preconception planning
- advise folic acid.

The team should plan a supervised switch to an alternative before conception. Options include an antipsychotic such as quetiapine or olanzapine (monitor for gestational diabetes and weight gain), or lithium with specialist input. Lithium carries a small increased risk of cardiac malformation and needs close level monitoring in pregnancy, at delivery and after birth, because fluid shifts alter levels, plus neonatal monitoring. The decision should be shared and documented.

After delivery she faces a high risk of relapse and postpartum psychosis, given bipolar I and a previous episode triggered by sleep loss. The perinatal plan should include:
- obstetric care with perinatal psychiatry input
- protected sleep (partner support with night feeds)
- early-warning signs agreed with her and her partner
- close review in the first weeks postpartum
- clear crisis contacts and access to a mother and baby unit if needed.

Breastfeeding compatibility should be discussed with specialists in light of the chosen drug.

questions.q: How many UK units of alcohol are in a 750 ml bottle of wine at 12% ABV?
State the classic triad of Wernicke's encephalopathy, its cause and its immediate treatment. (4 marks)
markScheme: Confusion
Ataxia
Ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus (triad often incomplete)
Thiamine deficiency (e.g. alcohol dependence, malnutrition); treat urgently with parenteral thiamine, before glucose
questions.modelAnswer: The classic triad is confusion, ataxia and ophthalmoplegia (or nystagmus), although many patients have only one or two features. It is caused by thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, most often in alcohol dependence with poor nutrition, but also in hyperemesis, after bariatric surgery and in malnutrition. Treat urgently with parenteral (intravenous or intramuscular) thiamine, given before or with glucose, because glucose can precipitate or worsen it. Untreated, it can progress to Korsakoff syndrome.

questions.q: Mr Gary Holt, 52, is two days after an emergency appendicectomy. Overnight he became agitated, sweaty and tremulous, is picking at the bedclothes and says insects are crawling on the walls. Pulse 118, BP 160/95, temperature 37.9 °C. His wife says he drinks 'a bottle of vodka a day' and has never been in hospital before. (a) What is the most likely diagnosis and what are the differentials? (b) Outline immediate management. (c) What should happen before discharge? (14 marks)
markScheme: Likely alcohol withdrawal delirium (delirium tremens) ~48–72h after last drink
Features: autonomic hyperactivity, tremor, visual hallucinations, agitation, fluctuating consciousness
Differentials: sepsis/postoperative infection, hypoglycaemia, electrolyte disturbance, hypoxia, head injury, Wernicke's, other drug withdrawal
Recognise medical emergency; senior help; ABCDE; safe environment
Long-acting benzodiazepine (e.g. chlordiazepoxide) symptom-triggered/regimen, IV route if needed (no doses)
Parenteral thiamine (before glucose); check glucose
Investigations: bloods (FBC, U&E, Mg, phosphate, glucose, LFT, CRP), cultures, ECG
Fluids, electrolyte replacement (Mg, K, phosphate), monitor with withdrawal scale (e.g. CIWA-Ar)
Pre-discharge: assess dependence (AUDIT/SADQ), brief intervention/motivational interviewing
Referral to alcohol liaison/community services; relapse prevention drugs (acamprosate, naltrexone) discussed
Avoid discharging with large benzodiazepine supply; GP communication; DVLA advice if dependent
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The likeliest diagnosis is alcohol withdrawal delirium (delirium tremens). He has abruptly stopped heavy drinking (about 28 units a day if it is a 70 cl bottle at 40% ABV) on admission, and two days later has agitation, tremor, sweating, tachycardia, hypertension, low-grade fever, picking behaviour and visual hallucinations. Delirium tremens typically appears around 48–72 hours after the last drink.
